problem.text: A number $m$ is randomly selected from the set $\{11,13,15,17,19\}$, and a number $n$ is randomly selected from $\{1999,2000,2001,\ldots,2018\}$. What is the probability that $m^n$ has a units digit of $1$?

steps.title: Where to start: only the last digit of m matters
steps.body: The units digit of $m^n$ depends only on the units digit of $m$. There are $5$ choices of $m$ and $20$ choices of $n$, so $5\cdot 20=100$ equally likely pairs. Count the pairs that work, one value of $m$ at a time.

your_turn.prompt: For which $n$ does $15^n$ end in $1$? And $11^n$?
your_turn.answer: $15^n$ always ends in $5$, so never. $11^n$ always ends in $1$, so for all $20$ values of $n$.

steps.title: Find the repeating patterns
steps.body: Powers of $3$ end in $3, 9, 7, 1$, then repeat. Powers of $7$ end in $7, 9, 3, 1$, then repeat. So $13^n$ and $17^n$ end in $1$ exactly when $n$ is a multiple of $4$. Powers of $9$ end in $9, 1, 9, 1, \ldots$

your_turn.answer: When $n$ is even, since the pattern $9, 1$ repeats every $2$ steps.

steps.title: Count the good values of n
steps.body: Careful: $19$ works for every even $n$, not only multiples of $4$, so do not lump it in with $13$ and $17$. The list $1999, \ldots, 2018$ has $20$ numbers, so $10$ of them are even.

your_turn.prompt: How many multiples of $4$ are in $1999, \ldots, 2018$?

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: Add up the good pairs: $20$ for $m=11$, $5$ for $13$, $0$ for $15$, $5$ for $17$, and $10$ for $19$. That is $40$ out of $100$ pairs, so the probability is $\frac{40}{100}=\frac{2}{5}$. The answer is **(E)**.

wrong_choices.D: $\frac{7}{20}$ comes from treating $19$ like $13$ and $17$, counting only multiples of $4$ for it. But $19^n$ ends in $1$ for every even $n$.
wrong_choices.C: $\frac{3}{10}$ comes from leaving out the $19$ case entirely. Powers of $9$ end in $1$ every second time.

verification.verifier_notes: Passed adversarial verifier on first review.
